title: Ἐλπήνορος τάφος καὶ Κίρκης ὑποθῆκαι
titleEn: Elpenor’s Burial and Circe’s Counsel — Odyssey 12.1–100
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus and his men leave the river Oceanus and beach their ship on Circe’s island, where Dawn has her dwellings and the Sun his risings. At daybreak they fetch the body of Elpenor and give him a funeral: they cut logs, burn the body and his armour, heap a mound, and fix his oar on top. Circe comes with attendants carrying food and wine, calls them twice-dying for having gone down to Hades alive, and tells them to feast for the day; at nightfall she takes Odysseus aside, hears everything, and begins to tell him what lies ahead. She warns him first of the Sirens and shows how to hear them safely, then describes two ways: the Wandering Rocks, and a pair of crags where Scylla lives in a cave, with her twelve feet, six necks and three rows of teeth.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ποταμοῖο λίπεν ῥόον Ὠκεανοῖο
νηῦς, ἀπὸ δ’ ἵκετο κῦμα θαλάσσης εὐρυπόροιο
νῆσόν τ’ Αἰαίην, ὅθι τ’ Ἠοῦς ἠριγενείης
οἰκία καὶ χοροί εἰσι καὶ ἀντολαὶ Ἠελίοιο,
sentences.tr:
autar epei potamoio lipen rhoon Ōkeanoio
nēus, apo d’ hiketo kyma thalassēs euryporoio
nēson t’ Aiaiēn, hothi t’ Ēous ērigeneiēs
oikia kai choroi eisi kai antolai Ēelioio,
sentences.l:
But when it left the stream of the river Oceanus,
the ship, and came to the wave of the wide-wayed sea,
and to the Aeaean island, where of early-born Dawn
are the dwellings and dancing-grounds, and the risings of the Sun,
sentences.i: When the ship had left the stream of the river Oceanus and come to the swell of the wide-wayed sea, and to the Aeaean island, where early-born Dawn has her dwellings and dancing-grounds and the Sun his risings,
sentences.n: Book 12 resumes Odysseus’ tale to the Phaeacians; the ship has just crossed the river Oceanus. This is a clause of time, and the main verb comes in line 5. νηῦς is the Ionic form of Attic ναῦς. λίπεν and ἵκετο are past tenses without the augment, and ἀπὸ δ’ ἵκετο is the preverb ἀπό standing apart from its verb (tmesis; Attic ἀφίκετο ‘came to’), which takes the accusative κῦμα. Ὠκεανοῖο and Ἠελίοιο are genitives in -οιο; Ἠοῦς is the contracted genitive of Ἠώς ‘Dawn’, and ἠριγενείης is her stock epithet ‘early-born’. The island is Circe’s (lines 9 and 16 show it), and it lies where Dawn has her dwellings (οἰκία) and dancing-grounds (χοροί) and the Sun his risings (ἀντολαί), that is, in the east.

sentences.t:
νῆα μὲν ἔνθ’ ἐλθόντες ἐκέλσαμεν ἐν ψαμάθοισιν,
ἐκ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ βῆμεν ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης·
sentences.tr:
nēa men enth’ elthontes ekelsamen en psamathoisin,
ek de kai autoi bēmen epi rhēgmini thalassēs·
sentences.l:
the ship, there having come, we ran ashore in the sands,
and out too we ourselves stepped upon the surf-line of the sea.
sentences.i: Coming there, we ran the ship ashore on the sands, and we ourselves too stepped out onto the shore where the sea breaks.
sentences.n: The main clause: the ship is beached and the crew land. νῆα, ‘the ship’, is the object of ἐκέλσαμεν, the aorist of κέλλω ‘run a ship ashore’, and ἔνθ’ ἐλθόντες is ‘having come there’. ἐν ψαμάθοισιν is ‘in the sands’, with the dative plural ending -οισιν. In the second line ἐκ … βῆμεν is the preverb ἐκ standing apart from its verb (tmesis, ‘stepped out’), and βῆμεν is the first plural aorist of βαίνω without the augment. ῥηγμῖνι is the dative of ῥηγμίς, the strip of shore where the waves break, and the house rendering keeps that image. These two lines are repeated from earlier in the poem, and the English follows the earlier renderings.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἀποβρίξαντες ἐμείναμεν Ἠῶ δῖαν.
sentences.tr: entha d’ apobrixantes emeinamen Ēō dian.
sentences.l: And there, having slept, we waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.i: There we slept and waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.n: A single line closes the landing. ἀποβρίξαντες is the aorist participle of ἀποβρίζω, a rare verb whose exact sense is not known; ‘having slept’ is taken from the context. ἐμείναμεν is the aorist of μένω ‘wait’, and Ἠῶ δῖαν is the accusative ‘heavenly Dawn’, δῖος being ‘heavenly’ by house rule.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
δὴ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἑτάρους προΐειν ἐς δώματα Κίρκης
οἰσέμεναι νεκρόν, Ἐλπήνορα τεθνηῶτα.
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
dē tot’ egōn hetarous proïein es dōmata Kirkēs
oisemenai nekron, Elpēnora tethnēōta.
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
then indeed I sent my companions to the halls of Circe
to carry the corpse, Elpenor, who had died.
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, I sent my companions to the halls of Circe to fetch the body of Elpenor, who had died.
sentences.n: The next morning, and the burial of the dead man Elpenor. ἦμος δ’ … Ἠώς is the dawn line: ἦμος ‘when’, ἠριγένεια ‘early-born’ and ῥοδοδάκτυλος ‘rose-fingered’, both kept every time. δὴ τότ’ is ‘then indeed’. προΐειν is the first person imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’ (epic for προΐην), and ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. οἰσέμεναι is the future infinitive of φέρω (Attic οἴσειν) with the epic ending -έμεναι, here expressing purpose, ‘to carry’. Ἐλπήνορα is in apposition to νεκρόν, and τεθνηῶτα is the uncontracted perfect participle of θνῄσκω (Attic τεθνεῶτα), ‘who had died’. The body is at Circe’s house, which is why the men go to δώματα Κίρκης.

sentences.t:
φιτροὺς δ’ αἶψα ταμόντες, ὅθ’ ἀκροτάτη πρόεχ’ ἀκτή,
θάπτομεν ἀχνύμενοι θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέοντες.
sentences.tr:
phitrous d’ aipsa tamontes, hoth’ akrotatē proech’ aktē,
thaptomen achnymenoi thaleron kata dakry cheontes.
sentences.l:
And logs quickly having cut, where the headland jutted farthest out,
we buried him, grieving, an abundant tear shedding.
sentences.i: We quickly cut logs, at the place where the headland jutted farthest out, and buried him, grieving and shedding abundant tears.
sentences.n: The funeral begins. φιτρούς is ‘logs’, and ταμόντες is the aorist participle of τέμνω ‘cut’, which has the aorist stem ταμ-. ὅθ’ is ‘where’. πρόεχ’ is the imperfect of προέχω ‘jut out’, and ἀκροτάτη the superlative of ἄκρος, ‘topmost, outermost’; ‘farthest out’ is the sense taken here. θάπτομεν, an imperfect, covers the whole funeral, including the burning narrated in the next line, so ‘buried’ means ‘performed the funeral rites’. ἀχνύμενοι is ‘grieving’, and κατὰ … χέοντες is the preverb κατά standing apart from its verb (tmesis), ‘shedding down’, with θαλερὸν δάκρυ ‘an abundant tear’, the singular used for tears in general.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ νεκρός τ’ ἐκάη καὶ τεύχεα νεκροῦ,
τύμβον χεύαντες καὶ ἐπὶ στήλην ἐρύσαντες
πήξαμεν ἀκροτάτῳ τύμβῳ ἐυῆρες ἐρετμόν.
sentences.tr:
autar epei nekros t’ ekaē kai teuchea nekrou,
tymbon cheuantes kai epi stēlēn erysantes
pēxamen akrotatōi tymbōi eyēres eretmon.
sentences.l:
But when the corpse was burned, and the armour of the dead man,
a mound having heaped up, and upon it a pillar having dragged up,
we fixed on the topmost mound the well-fitted oar.
sentences.i: When the body had burned, and the dead man’s armour with it, we heaped up a mound, dragged a pillar up onto it, and fixed the well-fitted oar on the very top of the mound.
sentences.n: The pyre, the mound and the marker. ἐκάη is the aorist passive of καίω ‘burn’, and τεύχεα, ‘armour, gear’, is burned with the dead man. χεύαντες is the aorist participle of χέω ‘pour’, used here of heaping up a mound; ἐπὶ … ἐρύσαντες is the preverb ἐπί apart from its verb (tmesis), ‘dragging up onto it’, from ἐρύω ‘drag’, and στήλη is an upright pillar or slab. πήξαμεν is the aorist of πήγνυμι ‘fix’. ἐυῆρες ἐρετμόν is ‘well-fitted oar’, with ἐυήρης from the root of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, and ἀκροτάτῳ τύμβῳ is the dative ‘on the very top of the mound’.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς μὲν τὰ ἕκαστα διείπομεν·
sentences.tr: hēmeis men ta hekasta dieipomen·
sentences.l: We, for our part, were carrying through each thing;
sentences.i: We were seeing to every detail;
sentences.n: διείπομεν is the imperfect of διέπω ‘carry through, attend to’, and τὰ ἕκαστα is ‘each of the several things’, here the rites just described. The sense ‘carry through’ is taken from the context. μὲν sets what the men were doing against what Circe does next, and the unit stops at the raised point in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα Κίρκην
ἐξ Ἀίδεω ἐλθόντες ἐλήθομεν, ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ὦκα
ἦλθ’ ἐντυναμένη·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara Kirkēn
ex Aideō elthontes elēthomen, alla mal’ ōka
ēlth’ entynamenē·
sentences.i: Nor did we escape Circe’s notice when we came back from Hades, but very quickly she came, her preparations made;
sentences.n: λανθάνω ‘escape the notice of’ takes the person in the accusative with a participle, so οὐδ’ … Κίρκην … ἐλήθομεν ἐλθόντες is ‘we did not come without Circe’s knowing’, literally ‘we did not escape Circe, having come’. ἐξ Ἀίδεω is ‘from Hades’, with the epic genitive Ἀίδεω. ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ὦκα is ‘but very quickly’. ἦλθ’ is ἦλθε elided. ἐντυναμένη is the aorist middle participle of ἐντύνω ‘make ready’; the Greek does not say whether she made ready herself or what she brings, so ‘her preparations made’ is kept open. The unit stops at the raised point in the middle of line 18.

sentences.t:
ἅμα δ’ ἀμφίπολοι φέρον αὐτῇ
σῖτον καὶ κρέα πολλὰ καὶ αἴθοπα οἶνον ἐρυθρόν.
sentences.tr:
hama d’ amphipoloi pheron autēi
siton kai krea polla kai aithopa oinon erythron.
sentences.l:
and together with her, attendants were carrying
food and much meat and fire-faced wine, red.
sentences.i: and with her came attendants carrying food, plenty of meat, and the red wine that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: ἅμα … αὐτῇ is ‘together with her’, ἀμφίπολοι ‘attendants’, and φέρον the imperfect of φέρω without the augment. σῖτον is ‘food’ and κρέα πολλά ‘much meat’ (neuter plural of κρέας). The wine is αἴθοπα οἶνον ἐρυθρόν: αἴθοψ, ‘fire-faced’, is the stock adjective of wine, kept as ‘the wine that has the look of fire’, and ἐρυθρόν is simply ‘red’.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἐν μέσσῳ στᾶσα μετηύδα δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: hē d’ en messōi stasa metēuda dia theaōn·
sentences.l: And she, in the midst having stood, spoke among them, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: And she, heavenly even among goddesses, stood in the midst and spoke among them:
sentences.n: The speech introduction, ending in a raised point because the speech follows. ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, the article as a pronoun, and στᾶσα is the aorist participle of ἵστημι ‘having stood’. μετηύδα is the imperfect of μεταυδάω ‘speak among’. δῖα θεάων is the stock epithet of a goddess, here of Circe: δῖα ‘heavenly’, and θεάων the genitive plural of θεά with the epic ending -άων, so ‘heavenly even among goddesses’.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιοι, οἳ ζώοντες ὑπήλθετε δῶμ’ Ἀίδαο,
δισθανέες, ὅτε τ’ ἄλλοι ἅπαξ θνῄσκουσ’ ἄνθρωποι.
sentences.tr:
schetlioi, hoi zōontes hypēlthete dōm’ Aidao,
disthanees, hote t’ alloi hapax thnēiskous’ anthrōpoi.
sentences.l:
‘Cruel ones, who living went down into the house of Hades,
twice-dying, when other men die once only.
sentences.i: ‘Cruel ones, you who went down alive into the house of Hades, men who die twice, when other men die only once.
sentences.n: Circe’s first speech begins. The Greek prints no quotation marks; the English opens a single mark, because Odysseus’ own tale is still being told and her words are a speech within it. σχέτλιοι is the vocative plural of σχέτλιος, kept as ‘cruel’ by house rule, though here it is an exclamation of dismay at what they have done, as the clause that follows shows. οἳ ζώοντες ὑπήλθετε is ‘you who, living, went down into’: ὑπήλθετε is the aorist of ὑπέρχομαι, and Ἀίδαο is the epic genitive of Ἀΐδης, so δῶμ’ Ἀίδαο is ‘the house of Hades’. δισθανέες is ‘twice-dying’ (δίς ‘twice’ + θνῄσκω), the uncontracted nominative plural (Attic δισθανεῖς). ὅτε τ’ ἄλλοι ἅπαξ θνῄσκουσ’ ἄνθρωποι is ‘when other men die once’, the epic τε marking a general truth.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ ἐσθίετε βρώμην καὶ πίνετε οἶνον
αὖθι πανημέριοι·
sentences.tr:
all’ aget’ esthiete brōmēn kai pinete oinon
authi panēmerioi·
sentences.l:
But come, eat food and drink wine
here on the spot, all the day;
sentences.i: But come, eat food and drink wine here all day long;
sentences.n: Her welcome turns to orders. ἄγετ’ is the plural imperative of ἄγω used as ‘come now’, and ἐσθίετε and πίνετε are plural imperatives; βρώμη is ‘food’. The first line is word for word the invitation Circe gave at 10.460. αὖθι is ‘right here’, and πανημέριοι ‘all day long’, nominative plural agreeing with the ‘you’ addressed. The unit stops at the raised point in the middle of line 24.

sentences.t:
ἅμα δ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι
πλεύσεσθ’·
sentences.tr:
hama d’ ēoi phainomenēphi
pleusesth’·
sentences.l:
and with dawn appearing
you will sail;
sentences.i: and when dawn appears you will sail;
sentences.n: ἅμα δ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι is ‘and with dawn appearing’, that is, at first light. ἠοῖ is the dative of ἠώς, and φαινομένηφι is a participle with the ending -φι, here standing for a dative (Attic φαινομένῃ). πλεύσεσθ’ is πλεύσεσθε elided, the future middle of πλέω ‘sail’. The unit is short because both of its ends fall at raised points in the middle of a line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ δείξω ὁδὸν ἠδὲ ἕκαστα
σημανέω, ἵνα μή τι κακορραφίῃ ἀλεγεινῇ
ἢ ἁλὸς ἢ ἐπὶ γῆς ἀλγήσετε πῆμα παθόντες.
sentences.tr:
autar egō deixō hodon ēde hekasta
sēmaneō, hina mē ti kakorraphiēi alegeinēi
ē halos ē epi gēs algēsete pēma pathontes.
sentences.l:
but I will show the way, and each thing
I will point out, so that not at all through grievous ill-contriving
either on the salt-sea or on land you may feel pain, having suffered woe.’
sentences.i: But I will show you the way and point out every detail, so that you do not, through some grievous bad planning, suffer pain and woe, on the sea or on land.’
sentences.n: Circe promises directions. δείξω and σημανέω are futures, the second uncontracted (Attic σημανῶ), ‘I will show … I will point out’, and ἕκαστα is ‘each thing, every detail’. ἵνα μή τι introduces the purpose, with ἀλγήσετε, from ἀλγέω ‘feel pain’, a short-vowel subjunctive (Attic ἀλγήσητε). κακορραφίῃ is a rare word built on κακός ‘bad’ and ῥάπτω ‘stitch’, so ‘bad contriving’, and ἀλεγεινῇ ‘grievous’ agrees with it; whose contriving it is, the Greek does not say. ἢ ἁλὸς ἢ ἐπὶ γῆς is ‘either on the salt-sea or on land’, ἁλός being the genitive of ἅλς. πῆμα παθόντες is ‘having suffered woe’. The speech ends here, and the English closes the single mark.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἡμῖν δ’ αὖτ’ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hēmin d’ aut’ epepeitheto thymos agēnōr.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and then our own lordly heart was persuaded;
sentences.i: So she said, and our own proud hearts were won over.
sentences.n: The speech is closed by narration. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so she spoke’ (ἔφατο elided), and ἡμῖν is a dative of interest, ‘to us’, so ‘our heart’. ἐπεπείθετο is the imperfect of ἐπιπείθομαι ‘obey, be persuaded’, with the preverb ἐπι-, the augment and the stem πείθ-. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is the stock phrase for the heart, ἀγήνωρ meaning ‘manly, proud’. The line is repeated from earlier in the poem and keeps its earlier English.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε μὲν πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα
ἥμεθα δαινύμενοι κρέα τ’ ἄσπετα καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ·
sentences.tr:
hōs tote men propan ēmar es ēelion katadynta
hēmetha dainymenoi krea t’ aspeta kai methy hēdy·
sentences.l:
So then for the whole day, until the sun going down,
we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.i: So for that whole day, until the sun went down, we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.n: A feasting day. πρόπαν ἦμαρ is an accusative of duration, ‘the whole day’. ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα is ‘until the sun went down’, with καταδύντα the aorist participle of καταδύω. ἥμεθα is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’ and δαινύμενοι ‘feasting’. ἄσπετα is ‘boundless’, literally ‘not to be told’, and μέθυ ἡδύ is ‘sweet wine’. These two lines are repeated from earlier in the poem and keep their earlier English.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠέλιος κατέδυ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἦλθεν,
οἱ μὲν κοιμήσαντο παρὰ πρυμνήσια νηός,
ἡ δ’ ἐμὲ χειρὸς ἑλοῦσα φίλων ἀπονόσφιν ἑταίρων
εἷσέ τε καὶ προσέλεκτο καὶ ἐξερέεινεν ἕκαστα·
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ēelios katedy kai epi knephas ēlthen,
hoi men koimēsanto para prymnēsia nēos,
hē d’ eme cheiros helousa philōn aponosphin hetairōn
heise te kai proselekto kai exereeinen hekasta·
sentences.l:
And when the sun set and darkness came on,
they, for their part, lay down to sleep beside the stern-cables of the ship,
but she, me by the hand having taken, apart from my dear companions,
seated me and lay down beside me and asked about each thing;
sentences.i: And when the sun set and darkness came on, they lay down to sleep beside the stern-cables of the ship, but she took me by the hand, away from my dear companions, seated me, lay down beside me, and asked about everything;
sentences.n: Evening, and Circe takes Odysseus apart. οἱ μὲν … ἡ δ’ sets the men against Circe. κοιμήσαντο is the aorist middle of κοιμάω ‘lay down to sleep’, and πρυμνήσια are the stern-cables. ἑλοῦσα is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take’, and it governs χειρός, a genitive of the part held, so ‘by the hand’; ἀπονόσφιν takes the genitive, ‘apart from’. εἷσε is the aorist of ἵζω in its causative sense, ‘made sit’. προσέλεκτο is taken here as the aorist middle of λέγω ‘lay down’, with πρός ‘beside’; some read it as ‘conversed with’, so the sense is not certain. ἐξερέεινεν is the imperfect of ἐξερεείνω ‘ask about’, and ἕκαστα ‘each thing’. The first line is repeated from earlier in the poem.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ τῇ πάντα κατὰ μοῖραν κατέλεξα.
sentences.tr: autar egō tēi panta kata moiran katelexa.
sentences.l: But I to her everything according to what is fitting recounted.
sentences.i: And I told her everything, as was fitting.
sentences.n: κατέλεξα is the aorist of καταλέγω ‘recount in full’. τῇ is ‘to her’, the article as a pronoun in the dative, and πάντα ‘everything’. κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘according to what is fitting’, μοῖρα being a due share or proper order.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε δή μ’ ἐπέεσσι προσηύδα πότνια Κίρκη·
sentences.tr: kai tote dē m’ epeessi prosēuda potnia Kirkē·
sentences.l: And then indeed me with words spoke the lady Circe:
sentences.i: And then the lady Circe spoke to me:
sentences.n: The speech introduction, closed by a raised point because the speech follows. καὶ τότε δή is ‘and then indeed’, and μ’ is με ‘me’. ἐπέεσσι is the dative plural of ἔπος, ‘with words’ (Attic ἔπεσι), and προσηύδα the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. πότνια is ‘lady’, the title of a goddess.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα μὲν οὕτω πάντα πεπείρανται, σὺ δ’ ἄκουσον,
ὥς τοι ἐγὼν ἐρέω, μνήσει δέ σε καὶ θεὸς αὐτός.
sentences.tr:
tauta men houtō panta pepeirantai, sy d’ akouson,
hōs toi egōn ereō, mnēsei de se kai theos autos.
sentences.l:
‘These things indeed thus all have been brought to an end; but you, listen,
as I will tell you, and a god himself will remind you.
sentences.i: ‘All this has now been brought to its end; but listen to what I shall tell you, and a god himself will remind you of it.
sentences.n: Circe’s second speech begins and runs on beyond this part, so the English opens a single mark and does not close it here. The Greek prints none. πεπείρανται is the perfect passive of περαίνω ‘bring to an end’, and ἄκουσον the aorist imperative of ἀκούω. ὥς τοι ἐγὼν ἐρέω is ‘as I shall tell you’, with ἐρέω the uncontracted future of the verb ἔρω (Attic ἐρῶ). μνήσει is the future of μιμνῄσκω in its sense ‘remind’, with σε ‘you’; the god is not named, only ‘a god himself’.

sentences.t:
Σειρῆνας μὲν πρῶτον ἀφίξεαι, αἵ ῥά τε πάντας
ἀνθρώπους θέλγουσιν, ὅτις σφεας εἰσαφίκηται.
sentences.tr:
Seirēnas men prōton aphixeai, hai rha te pantas
anthrōpous thelgousin, hotis spheas eisaphikētai.
sentences.l:
To the Sirens first you will come, who all
men enchant, whoever arrives at them.
sentences.i: You will come first to the Sirens, who enchant all men, whoever comes to them.
sentences.n: The first danger. ἀφίξεαι is the future middle of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive’ with the uncontracted ending -εαι (Attic ἀφίξῃ). Σειρῆνας is the accusative plural of Σειρήν. αἵ ῥά τε is the relative ‘who’ with the particles ῥα and the epic τε that marks a general truth. θέλγουσιν is ‘enchant’ by house rule. ὅτις … εἰσαφίκηται is a general clause, ‘whoever comes to them’, the aorist subjunctive of εἰσαφικνέομαι, and σφεας is ‘them’ (Attic σφᾶς).

sentences.t:
ὅς τις ἀιδρείῃ πελάσῃ καὶ φθόγγον ἀκούσῃ
Σειρήνων, τῷ δ’ οὔ τι γυνὴ καὶ νήπια τέκνα
οἴκαδε νοστήσαντι παρίσταται οὐδὲ γάνυνται,
sentences.tr:
hos tis aidreiēi pelasēi kai phthongon akousēi
Seirēnōn, tōi d’ ou ti gynē kai nēpia tekna
oikade nostēsanti paristatai oude ganyntai,
sentences.l:
Whoever in ignorance draws near and hears the voice
of the Sirens, to him no wife and infant children
stand beside him, returned home, nor do they rejoice,
sentences.i: Whoever draws near them in ignorance and hears the voice of the Sirens, no wife and infant children stand beside him when he has come home, and they do not rejoice,
sentences.n: The sentence is long, so it is cut at a comma. ὅς τις is ὅστις, the general relative, with the subjunctives πελάσῃ and ἀκούσῃ (Homer often leaves out ἄν or κε here): ‘whoever draws near … and hears’. ἀιδρείῃ is ‘in ignorance’ (ἀ- and the root of οἶδα ‘know’). Σειρήνων is the genitive plural. The main clause is τῷ … γυνὴ καὶ νήπια τέκνα … παρίσταται οὐδὲ γάνυνται: τῷ is ‘to him’, νήπια τέκνα ‘infant children’, παρίσταται ‘stands beside’ (singular, agreeing with γυνή) and γάνυνται ‘they rejoice’ (plural). οἴκαδε is ‘homeward’, with the suffix -δε of direction, and νοστήσαντι the aorist participle of νοστέω ‘return home’, agreeing with τῷ.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τε Σειρῆνες λιγυρῇ θέλγουσιν ἀοιδῇ
ἥμεναι ἐν λειμῶνι, πολὺς δ’ ἀμφ’ ὀστεόφιν θὶς
ἀνδρῶν πυθομένων, περὶ δὲ ῥινοὶ μινύθουσι.
sentences.tr:
alla te Seirēnes ligyrēi thelgousin aoidēi
hēmenai en leimōni, polys d’ amph’ osteophin this
andrōn pythomenōn, peri de rhinoi minythousi.
sentences.l:
but the Sirens enchant him with a clear song,
sitting in a meadow, and a great heap around the bones
of rotting men, and about them the skins shrivel.
sentences.i: but the Sirens enchant him with their clear song, sitting in a meadow; and all about them lies a great heap of the bones of rotting men, with the skins shrivelling on them.
sentences.n: ἀλλά τε is ‘but’ with the epic τε; the object of θέλγουσιν, ‘him’, is understood. λιγυρῇ is ‘clear-sounding’, and ἥμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἧμαι ‘sit’, here ‘as they sit’. πολὺς … θίς is ‘a great heap’, and ἀμφ’ ὀστεόφιν has the ending -φι on ὀστέον ‘bone’, so ‘around the bones’. πυθομένων is the participle of πύθομαι ‘rot’, not of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn’. ῥινοί are ‘skins’, and μινύθουσι is ‘waste away, shrivel’. The Greek does not say who the dead men are; they are those who listened.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ παρεξελάαν, ἐπὶ δ’ οὔατ’ ἀλεῖψαι ἑταίρων
κηρὸν δεψήσας μελιηδέα, μή τις ἀκούσῃ
τῶν ἄλλων·
sentences.tr:
alla parexelaan, epi d’ ouat’ aleipsai hetairōn
kēron depsēsas meliēdea, mē tis akousēi
tōn allōn·
sentences.i: But drive on past, and smear the ears of your companions with honey-sweet wax that you have kneaded, so that none of the others may hear;
sentences.n: Circe’s advice. παρεξελάαν and ἀλεῖψαι are infinitives used as commands, ‘drive past’ and ‘smear’, addressed to Odysseus; ἐλάαν is the uncontracted form of ἐλαύνειν. ἐπὶ … ἀλεῖψαι is the preverb ἐπί standing apart from its verb (tmesis). οὔατα is ‘ears’ (accusative plural of οὖς). δεψήσας is the aorist participle of δέψω ‘knead’, κηρόν ‘wax’, and μελιηδέα ‘honey-sweet’ by house rule. μή τις ἀκούσῃ is ‘lest anyone hear’, with the aorist subjunctive, and τῶν ἄλλων is a partitive genitive with τις, ‘any of the others’, which the line-break separates from it. The unit stops at the raised point in the middle of line 49.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ αὐτὸς ἀκουέμεν αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα,
δησάντων σ’ ἐν νηὶ θοῇ χεῖράς τε πόδας τε
ὀρθὸν ἐν ἱστοπέδῃ, ἐκ δ’ αὐτοῦ πείρατ’ ἀνήφθω,
ὄφρα κε τερπόμενος ὄπ’ ἀκούσῃς Σειρήνοιιν.
sentences.tr:
atar autos akouemen ai k’ ethelēistha,
dēsantōn s’ en nēi thoēi cheiras te podas te
orthon en histopedēi, ek d’ autou peirat’ anēphthō,
ophra ke terpomenos op’ akousēis Seirēnoiin.
sentences.l:
but you yourself, if you wish to hear,
let them bind you in the swift ship, hands and feet,
upright in the mast-step, and from it let the rope-ends be fastened,
that you may hear, delighting, the voice of the two Sirens.
sentences.i: But you yourself, if you wish to hear, have them bind you hand and foot in the swift ship, upright in the mast-step, and let the ends of the ropes be fastened from it, so that you may listen in delight to the voice of the two Sirens.
sentences.n: ἀκουέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἀκούω, and αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is ‘if you wish’, with the epic ending -σθα and κε. δησάντων is the third plural aorist imperative of δέω ‘bind’, so ‘let them bind’; χεῖράς τε πόδας τε ‘hands and feet’ are accusatives of the part bound. ἱστοπέδῃ is the mast-step, the socket for the mast. ἐκ δ’ αὐτοῦ πείρατ’ ἀνήφθω is ‘and from it let the rope-ends be fastened’, ἀνήφθω being the perfect passive imperative of ἀνάπτω. αὐτοῦ is masculine, so it cannot be the feminine ἱστοπέδη; it means the mast, which ἱστο- implies, or Odysseus himself. ὄφρα κε … ἀκούσῃς is a purpose clause, ὄπ’ is ὄπα, the accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’, and Σειρήνοιιν is a dual genitive, ‘of the two Sirens’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε λίσσηαι ἑτάρους λῦσαί τε κελεύῃς,
οἱ δέ σ’ ἔτι πλεόνεσσι τότ’ ἐν δεσμοῖσι διδέντων.
sentences.tr:
ei de ke lissēai hetarous lysai te keleuēis,
hoi de s’ eti pleonessi tot’ en desmoisi didentōn.
sentences.l:
But if you beg your companions and bid them loose you,
let them then bind you in still more bonds.
sentences.i: But if you beg your companions, and order them to set you free, then let them bind you with still more bonds.
sentences.n: εἰ δέ κε is ‘but if’, with κε, and λίσσηαι and κελεύῃς are subjunctives, the first uncontracted (Attic λίσσῃ): ‘you beg … and bid’. λῦσαι is the aorist infinitive of λύω ‘loose’. In the second line οἱ is ‘they’, σ’ is σε, and διδέντων is the third plural imperative of δίδημι, an athematic by-form of δέω ‘bind’. ἔτι πλεόνεσσι … δεσμοῖσι is ‘in still more bonds’, with the dative plural ending -εσσι.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν δὴ τάς γε παρὲξ ἐλάσωσιν ἑταῖροι,
ἔνθα τοι οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτα διηνεκέως ἀγορεύσω,
ὁπποτέρη δή τοι ὁδὸς ἔσσεται, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸς
θυμῷ βουλεύειν·
sentences.tr:
autar epēn dē tas ge parex elasōsin hetairoi,
entha toi ouket’ epeita diēnekeōs agoreusō,
hoppoterē dē toi hodos essetai, alla kai autos
thymōi bouleuein·
sentences.l:
But when your companions have driven past these,
then to you no longer after that continuously will I speak,
which of the two roads indeed will be yours, but you yourself also
in your heart must plan;
sentences.i: But when your companions have driven past these, then I will no longer tell you in full which of the two ways will be yours; you must also decide that yourself, in your heart;
sentences.n: From here Circe stops directing and leaves a choice to Odysseus. ἐπὴν δή … ἐλάσωσιν is ‘when … they have driven’, an aorist subjunctive, and παρὲξ is ‘past, beyond’; τάς γε is ‘these’, the Sirens. διηνεκέως is ‘continuously, in full’, and ἀγορεύσω is the future of ἀγορεύω ‘speak’. ὁπποτέρη is ‘which of the two’, so there are two roads, and ἔσσεται is the future of εἰμί. ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸς θυμῷ βουλεύειν is an infinitive with the force of a command, ‘you yourself must also plan in your heart’. The unit stops at the raised point in the middle of line 58.

sentences.t: ἐρέω δέ τοι ἀμφοτέρωθεν.
sentences.tr: ereō de toi amphoterōthen.
sentences.l: and I will tell you of both sides.
sentences.i: but I will tell you of both sides.
sentences.n: ἐρέω is the uncontracted future of ἔρω, ‘I will tell’, and ἀμφοτέρωθεν is ‘from both sides’, with the suffix -θεν. She will not choose for him, but she will describe each side. The unit is the second half of line 58.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν μὲν γὰρ πέτραι ἐπηρεφέες, προτὶ δ’ αὐτὰς
κῦμα μέγα ῥοχθεῖ κυανώπιδος Ἀμφιτρίτης·
sentences.tr:
enthen men gar petrai epērephees, proti d’ autas
kyma mega rhochthei kyanōpidos Amphitritēs·
sentences.l:
For on one side overhanging rocks, and against them
a great wave roars of dark-eyed Amphitrite;
sentences.i: For on the one side are overhanging rocks, and against them roars the great wave of dark-eyed Amphitrite;
sentences.n: The first of the two ways. ἔνθεν μὲν γάρ is ‘for on one side’, and ἐπηρεφέες is ‘overhanging’. προτί is πρός, and αὐτάς is ‘them’. ῥοχθεῖ is the third singular of ῥοχθέω ‘roar, dash noisily’, said of breakers. κυανώπιδος is the genitive of κυανῶπις ‘dark-eyed’, built on κύανος ‘dark blue’ and ὤψ ‘eye’; Ἀμφιτρίτη is a sea-goddess, and her name here stands for the sea. The unit ends at the raised point.

sentences.t: Πλαγκτὰς δή τοι τάς γε θεοὶ μάκαρες καλέουσι.
sentences.tr: Planktas dē toi tas ge theoi makares kaleousi.
sentences.l: the Wandering Rocks, indeed, these the blessed gods call.
sentences.i: The blessed gods call these the Wandering Rocks.
sentences.n: Πλαγκτάς is the accusative feminine plural of πλαγκτός ‘wandering, driven astray’, from πλάζω; with πέτρας understood from line 59 it is the name of the rocks, ‘the Wandering Rocks’. δή τοι is ‘indeed, I tell you’, and τάς γε ‘these’. θεοὶ μάκαρες is ‘the blessed gods’, and καλέουσι is the uncontracted form of καλοῦσι ‘call’.

sentences.t:
τῇ μέν τ’ οὐδὲ ποτητὰ παρέρχεται οὐδὲ πέλειαι
τρήρωνες, ταί τ’ ἀμβροσίην Διὶ πατρὶ φέρουσιν,
ἀλλά τε καὶ τῶν αἰὲν ἀφαιρεῖται λὶς πέτρη·
sentences.tr:
tēi men t’ oude potēta parerchetai oude peleiai
trērōnes, tai t’ ambrosiēn Dii patri pherousin,
alla te kai tōn aien aphaireitai lis petrē·
sentences.i: No winged creature passes that way, not even the timorous doves that carry ambrosia to father Zeus; the smooth rock always takes one of them away;
sentences.n: τῇ is ‘by that way’, and ποτητά, the neuter plural of ποτητός ‘flying’, is ‘winged things’. οὐδὲ … οὐδέ is ‘not even … nor’. πέλειαι are doves, and τρήρωνες ‘timorous’ is their epithet. ἀμβροσίην is ‘ambrosia’, the food of the gods, carried Διὶ πατρί ‘to father Zeus’. ἀλλά τε καὶ τῶν is ‘but even of these’. ἀφαιρεῖται is middle, ‘takes away for itself’, and the object ‘one’ is understood. λὶς πέτρη is ‘the smooth rock’: λίς is an adjective ‘smooth, bare’. The unit ends at the raised point.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄλλην ἐνίησι πατὴρ ἐναρίθμιον εἶναι.
sentences.tr: all’ allēn eniēsi patēr enarithmion einai.
sentences.l: but another the father sends in, to be one of the number.
sentences.i: but the father sends in another, to keep the number complete.
sentences.n: ἐνίησι is ‘sends in’, the present of ἐνίημι. πατήρ is Zeus, named as ‘father Zeus’ at line 63. ἐναρίθμιον εἶναι is ‘to be counted in, to make up the number’: the rock takes one dove, and another is sent to replace it.

sentences.t:
τῇ δ’ οὔ πώ τις νηῦς φύγεν ἀνδρῶν, ἥ τις ἵκηται,
ἀλλά θ’ ὁμοῦ πίνακάς τε νεῶν καὶ σώματα φωτῶν
κύμαθ’ ἁλὸς φορέουσι πυρός τ’ ὀλοοῖο θύελλαι.
sentences.tr:
tēi d’ ou pō tis nēus phygen andrōn, hē tis hikētai,
alla th’ homou pinakas te neōn kai sōmata phōtōn
kymath’ halos phoreousi pyros t’ olooio thyellai.
sentences.l:
And from there not yet has any ship of men escaped, whichever has come,
but together planks of ships and bodies of men
the waves of the salt-sea carry, and the storm-blasts of deadly fire.
sentences.i: And no ship of men that has come there has yet escaped; the waves of the sea carry off the planks of ships and the bodies of men together, and so do the storm-blasts of deadly fire.
sentences.n: What happens to ships that reach the rocks. τῇ here is ‘there’, so ‘has escaped from there’. φύγεν is an unaugmented aorist of φεύγω. ἥ τις ἵκηται is ‘whichever comes’, a relative with indefinite τις and the aorist subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι. πίνακας are ‘planks’, νεῶν is the genitive plural of ναῦς (the form is the same in Attic), and φωτῶν the genitive plural of φώς ‘man’. κύμαθ’ is κύματα, ‘waves’, and φορέουσι is the uncontracted form of φοροῦσι ‘carry’; the subjects are κύματα and θύελλαι, ‘storm-blasts’, here πυρὸς ὀλοοῖο ‘of deadly fire’.

sentences.t:
οἴη δὴ κείνη γε παρέπλω ποντοπόρος νηῦς,
Ἀργὼ πᾶσι μέλουσα, παρ’ Αἰήταο πλέουσα.
sentences.tr:
oiē dē keinē ge pareplō pontoporos nēus,
Argō pasi melousa, par’ Aiētao pleousa.
sentences.l:
Alone indeed that one sailed past, the sea-crossing ship,
Argo, a care to all, sailing from Aeetes.
sentences.i: Only that one sea-crossing ship has ever sailed past there, Argo, of concern to all, on her way from Aeetes.
sentences.n: οἴη is ‘alone, the only one’, and κείνη γε ‘that one’. παρέπλω is ‘sailed past’, an aorist of παραπλέω of the root type (Attic παρέπλευσε). ποντοπόρος is ‘sea-crossing’, from πόντος ‘open sea’ and πόρος ‘passage’. Ἀργώ is the ship Argo, and πᾶσι μέλουσα is ‘being a care to all’; the Greek says no more than that all were concerned with her. παρ’ Αἰήταο πλέουσα is ‘sailing from Aeetes’, with παρά and the genitive meaning ‘from beside’ and Αἰήταο the epic genitive of Αἰήτης.

sentences.t:
καὶ νύ κε τὴν ἔνθ’ ὦκα βάλεν μεγάλας ποτὶ πέτρας,
ἀλλ’ Ἥρη παρέπεμψεν, ἐπεὶ φίλος ἦεν Ἰήσων.
sentences.tr:
kai ny ke tēn enth’ ōka balen megalas poti petras,
all’ Hērē parepempsen, epei philos ēen Iēsōn.
sentences.l:
And even her there quickly would it have thrown against the great rocks,
but Hera sent her past, since dear to her was Jason.
sentences.i: And she would have been hurled quickly there against the great rocks, but Hera sent her past, because Jason was dear to her.
sentences.n: καὶ νύ κε … βάλεν is κε with an unaugmented aorist, ‘would have thrown’, a past event that did not happen; no subject is stated, only whatever drives ships onto the rocks, so the English turns it into a passive. τὴν is ‘her’, the ship, and ὦκα ‘quickly’. ἀλλ’ Ἥρη παρέπεμψεν is ‘but Hera sent her past’. ἐπεὶ φίλος ἦεν Ἰήσων is ‘since Jason was dear’, with ἦεν = ἦν and φίλος ‘dear’ to Hera.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ δύω σκόπελοι ὁ μὲν οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἱκάνει
ὀξείῃ κορυφῇ, νεφέλη δέ μιν ἀμφιβέβηκε
κυανέη·
sentences.tr:
hoi de dyō skopeloi ho men ouranon euryn hikanei
oxeiēi koryphēi, nephelē de min amphibebēke
kyaneē·
sentences.i: As for the two crags, the one reaches the broad heaven with its sharp peak, and a dark cloud has settled around it;
sentences.n: Circe turns to the other side, two crags; only the first is described in this part. οἱ δὲ δύω σκόπελοι is ‘and the two crags’, δύω being ‘two’ and σκόπελος a crag or rocky peak, and ὁ μέν is ‘the one’. ἱκάνει is ‘reaches’, and ὀξείῃ κορυφῇ is a dative of respect, ‘with a sharp peak’. μιν is ‘it’, and ἀμφιβέβηκε is a perfect of ἀμφιβαίνω with the sense ‘stands around, wraps’. κυανέη is ‘dark’. The unit stops at the raised point in the middle of line 75.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν οὔ ποτ’ ἐρωεῖ, οὐδέ ποτ’ αἴθρη
κείνου ἔχει κορυφὴν οὔτ’ ἐν θέρει οὔτ’ ἐν ὀπώρῃ.
sentences.tr:
to men ou pot’ erōei, oude pot’ aithrē
keinou echei koryphēn out’ en therei out’ en opōrēi.
sentences.l:
that never draws back, nor ever does clear sky
hold that one’s peak, neither in summer nor in late summer.
sentences.i: it never lifts, and clear sky never holds its peak, in summer or in late summer.
sentences.n: τὸ μὲν is neuter, so it is not the feminine cloud (νεφέλη) itself but the cloud-covering as a whole. ἐρωεῖ is ‘draws back, lets up’, from ἐρωέω. αἴθρη is ‘clear sky, bright air’, and κείνου ἔχει κορυφήν is ‘holds that one’s peak’, κείνου being the crag. θέρος is ‘summer’, and ὀπώρη the late summer when fruit ripens, which is not the English ‘autumn’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κεν ἀμβαίη βροτὸς ἀνὴρ οὐδ’ ἐπιβαίη,
οὐδ’ εἴ οἱ χεῖρές τε ἐείκοσι καὶ πόδες εἶεν·
sentences.tr:
oude ken ambaiē brotos anēr oud’ epibaiē,
oud’ ei hoi cheires te eeikosi kai podes eien·
sentences.l:
Nor could a mortal man climb up it, nor step upon it,
not even if twenty hands and feet were his;
sentences.i: No mortal man could climb it or set foot on it, not even if he had twenty hands and feet;
sentences.n: The summit cannot be climbed. οὐδέ κεν … ἀμβαίη … ἐπιβαίη is κε with aorist optatives, ‘could climb, could step on’, from ἀναβαίνω and ἐπιβαίνω; βροτὸς ἀνήρ is ‘a mortal man’. οὐδ’ εἰ … εἶεν is ‘not even if there were’, with οἱ ‘to him’ and εἶεν the optative of εἰμί. ἐείκοσι is εἴκοσι ‘twenty’, and χεῖρές τε … καὶ πόδες is ‘hands and feet’.

sentences.t: πέτρη γὰρ λίς ἐστι, περιξεστῇ ἐικυῖα.
sentences.tr: petrē gar lis esti, perixestēi eikuia.
sentences.l: for the rock is smooth, like to one polished all round.
sentences.i: for the rock is smooth, like something polished all round.
sentences.n: The reason: γάρ. πέτρη … λίς ἐστι is ‘the rock is smooth’, with λίς as in line 64. περιξεστῇ is the dative of περίξεστος ‘polished all round’, and ἐικυῖα, the perfect participle of ἔοικα, takes the dative: ‘like something polished all round’, the feminine περιξεστῇ agreeing with an understood πέτρῃ.

sentences.t:
μέσσῳ δ’ ἐν σκοπέλῳ ἔστι σπέος ἠεροειδές,
πρὸς ζόφον εἰς Ἔρεβος τετραμμένον, ᾗ περ ἂν ὑμεῖς
νῆα παρὰ γλαφυρὴν ἰθύνετε, φαίδιμ’ Ὀδυσσεῦ.
sentences.tr:
messōi d’ en skopelōi esti speos ēeroeides,
pros zophon eis Erebos tetrammenon, hēi per an hymeis
nēa para glaphyrēn ithynete, phaidim’ Odysseu.
sentences.l:
And in the middle of the crag is a misty-looking cave,
turned toward the gloom, to Erebus, where indeed you
will steer your hollow ship past, glorious Odysseus.
sentences.i: In the middle of the crag is a cave that looks misty, turned toward the gloom, toward Erebus, just where you will steer your hollow ship past, glorious Odysseus.
sentences.n: The cave in the crag. μέσσῳ ἐν σκοπέλῳ is ‘in the middle of the crag’, and σπέος ἠεροειδές is ‘a misty-looking cave’, built on ἀήρ ‘mist’. τετραμμένον is the perfect passive participle of τρέπω ‘turn’. ζόφος is ‘gloom’ and Ἔρεβος the place of darkness. ᾗ περ ἂν ὑμεῖς … ἰθύνετε is ‘just where you will steer’, with a short-vowel subjunctive, and παρά … is a preverb standing apart from ἰθύνετε, ‘steer past’. ὑμεῖς is plural, Odysseus and his crew together. φαίδιμ’ is φαίδιμε, ‘glorious’, the vocative, and the ship is νῆα … γλαφυρήν, ‘hollow’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κεν ἐκ νηὸς γλαφυρῆς αἰζήιος ἀνὴρ
τόξῳ ὀιστεύσας κοῖλον σπέος εἰσαφίκοιτο.
sentences.tr:
oude ken ek nēos glaphyrēs aizēios anēr
toxōi oisteusas koilon speos eisaphikoito.
sentences.l:
Nor could from a hollow ship a vigorous man
shooting with a bow reach the hollow cave.
sentences.i: Not even a vigorous man could shoot an arrow with a bow from a hollow ship and reach the hollow cave.
sentences.n: οὐδέ κεν … εἰσαφίκοιτο is ‘nor could … reach’, an optative with κε. αἰζήιος is ‘vigorous’, said of a man in the full strength of youth. τόξῳ ὀιστεύσας is ‘having shot an arrow with a bow’, from ὀιστεύω and ὀιστός ‘arrow’. νηός is the Ionic genitive of ναῦς, with γλαφυρῆς ‘hollow’, and the cave itself is κοῖλον, ‘hollow’.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἐνὶ Σκύλλη ναίει δεινὸν λελακυῖα.
sentences.tr: entha d’ eni Skyllē naiei deinon lelakuia.
sentences.l: And there within Scylla dwells, yelling dreadfully.
sentences.i: And within it Scylla dwells, shrieking dreadfully.
sentences.n: Scylla is named. ἔνθα δ’ ἐνὶ Σκύλλη ναίει is ‘and there within Scylla dwells’, ἐνί being an adverb ‘within’. δεινὸν λελακυῖα has δεινόν as an adverb, ‘dreadfully’, and λελακυῖα is the perfect participle of λάσκω ‘cry out, shriek’, a perfect with present sense; the next line compares her voice with that of a puppy, σκύλαξ.

sentences.t:
τῆς ἦ τοι φωνὴ μὲν ὅση σκύλακος νεογιλῆς
γίγνεται, αὐτὴ δ’ αὖτε πέλωρ κακόν·
sentences.tr:
tēs ē toi phōnē men hosē skylakos neogilēs
gignetai, autē d’ aute pelōr kakon·
sentences.l:
Her voice indeed is as great as a newborn puppy’s
becomes, but she herself in turn a monster, evil;
sentences.i: Her voice is just as big as a newborn puppy’s, but she herself is an evil monster;
sentences.n: τῆς ἦ τοι φωνή is ‘her voice, truly’. ὅση is ‘as great as’, with σκύλακος νεογιλῆς, ‘of a newborn puppy’; νεογιλός means ‘newborn’ but its second part is obscure. γίγνεται is ‘is, comes to be’. αὐτὴ δ’ αὖτε is ‘but she herself, in her turn’, and πέλωρ κακόν is ‘an evil monster’. The unit stops at the raised point in the middle of line 87.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κέ τίς μιν
γηθήσειεν ἰδών, οὐδ’ εἰ θεὸς ἀντιάσειεν.
sentences.tr:
oude ke tis min
gēthēseien idōn, oud’ ei theos antiaseien.
sentences.l:
and no one at the sight of her
would rejoice, not even if a god met her.
sentences.i: and nobody who saw her would be glad, not even if a god met her.
sentences.n: οὐδέ κέ τίς μιν γηθήσειεν ἰδών is ‘nor would anyone, seeing her, rejoice’, an optative with κε, with ἰδών the aorist participle of ὁράω and μιν ‘her’. οὐδ’ εἰ θεὸς ἀντιάσειεν is ‘not even if a god met her’, ἀντιάω ‘meet, encounter’ in the aorist optative.

sentences.t:
τῆς ἦ τοι πόδες εἰσὶ δυώδεκα πάντες ἄωροι,
ἓξ δέ τέ οἱ δειραὶ περιμήκεες, ἐν δὲ ἑκάστῃ
σμερδαλέη κεφαλή, ἐν δὲ τρίστοιχοι ὀδόντες
πυκνοὶ καὶ θαμέες, πλεῖοι μέλανος θανάτοιο.
sentences.tr:
tēs ē toi podes eisi dyōdeka pantes aōroi,
hex de te hoi deirai perimēkees, en de hekastēi
smerdaleē kephalē, en de tristoichoi odontes
pyknoi kai thamees, pleioi melanos thanatoio.
sentences.l:
Of her indeed the feet are twelve, all dangling,
and to her six necks, very long, and on each
a frightful head, and in them three rows of teeth,
close-packed and crowded, full of black death.
sentences.i: She has twelve feet, all of them dangling, and six very long necks, and on each a frightful head, and in each three rows of teeth, close-packed and crowded, full of black death.
sentences.n: Scylla’s body. τῆς ἦ τοι πόδες εἰσί is ‘her feet are’, and δυώδεκα is ‘twelve’. ἄωροι is a word whose meaning is not known; ‘dangling’ is a traditional guess, and ‘misshapen’ and ‘unseasonable’ have also been proposed. δειραί are ‘necks’, περιμήκεες ‘very long’, and σμερδαλέη ‘frightful’. τρίστοιχοι ὀδόντες is ‘teeth in three rows’, πυκνοί and θαμέες ‘close-packed’ and ‘crowded’, and πλεῖοι μέλανος θανάτοιο ‘full of black death’, with πλεῖοι the plural of πλεῖος ‘full’ and the genitive of what fills.

sentences.t:
μέσση μέν τε κατὰ σπείους κοίλοιο δέδυκεν,
ἔξω δ’ ἐξίσχει κεφαλὰς δεινοῖο βερέθρου,
sentences.tr:
messē men te kata speious koiloio dedyken,
exō d’ exischei kephalas deinoio berethrou,
sentences.l:
As to her middle, down in the hollow cave she has sunk,
but outside the dread pit she holds out her heads,
sentences.i: She has sunk down into the hollow cave up to her middle, and holds her heads out of the dread pit,
sentences.n: μέσση is feminine and agrees with Scylla, ‘in her middle’. μέν τε … δέ sets what is in the cave against what is outside. κατά with the genitive σπείους (a form of σπέος ‘cave’) means ‘down in’, and δέδυκεν is the perfect of δύω ‘sink’, ‘has sunk, is sunk’. ἔξω … ἐξίσχει is ‘outside … holds out’, with κεφαλάς ‘heads’ the accusative plural; ἔξω takes the genitive δεινοῖο βερέθρου, ‘out of the dread pit’, and βέρεθρον is a pit or chasm.

sentences.t:
αὐτοῦ δ’ ἰχθυάᾳ, σκόπελον περιμαιμώωσα,
δελφῖνάς τε κύνας τε, καὶ εἴ ποθι μεῖζον ἕλῃσι
κῆτος, ἃ μυρία βόσκει ἀγάστονος Ἀμφιτρίτη.
sentences.tr:
autou d’ ichthyaāi, skopelon perimaimōōsa,
delphinas te kynas te, kai ei pothi meizon helēisi
kētos, ha myria boskei agastonos Amphitritē.
sentences.i: and there she fishes, feeling all around the crag, for dolphins and dogs, and for any bigger sea-monster she may catch, of the countless ones that loud-groaning Amphitrite feeds.
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ is ‘right there’, and ἰχθυάᾳ is ‘she fishes’, from ἰχθυάω. σκόπελον περιμαιμώωσα is ‘feeling about around the crag’, περιμαιμώωσα being a participle of περιμαιμάω with the epic doubled vowel. δελφῖνας are dolphins; κύνας are ‘dogs’, some sea creature, and which one is meant is not known. καὶ εἴ ποθι μεῖζον ἕλῃσι κῆτος is ‘and if anywhere she catches a bigger sea-monster’, with μεῖζον agreeing with κῆτος across the line-end, and ἕλῃσι being the aorist subjunctive of αἱρέω. ἃ μυρία βόσκει is ‘which, countless, she feeds’, and ἀγάστονος, ‘loud-groaning’, is the epithet of Amphitrite, built on the intensive ἀγα- and στένω ‘groan’.

sentences.t:
τῇ δ’ οὔ πώ ποτε ναῦται ἀκήριοι εὐχετόωνται
παρφυγέειν σὺν νηί·
sentences.tr:
tēi d’ ou pō pote nautai akērioi euchetoōntai
parphygeein syn nēi·
sentences.l:
And there never yet do sailors uninjured declare
that they have escaped with their ship;
sentences.i: No sailors have yet declared that they slipped past there with their ship uninjured;
sentences.n: τῇ is ‘there’. ναῦται is ‘sailors’, and ἀκήριοι ‘uninjured’, from ἀ- and κήρ, the doom that destroys; the formation is not fully clear, and the sense ‘uninjured’ is taken from what the sentence needs. εὐχετόωνται is the third plural of εὐχετάομαι, a lengthened form of εὔχομαι ‘declare’, with the vowels left uncontracted (Attic εὐχετῶνται), and παρφυγέειν the aorist infinitive of παραφεύγω ‘escape past’ (Attic παραφυγεῖν). σὺν νηί is ‘with their ship’. The unit stops at the raised point in the middle of line 99.

sentences.t:
φέρει δέ τε κρατὶ ἑκάστῳ
φῶτ’ ἐξαρπάξασα νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο.
sentences.tr:
pherei de te krati hekastōi
phōt’ exarpaxasa neos kyanoprōiroio.
sentences.l:
for she carries off, with each head,
a man, snatching him from the dark-prowed ship.
sentences.i: for with each head she carries off a man, snatching him out of a dark-prowed ship.
sentences.n: φέρει δέ τε is ‘for she carries off’. κρατί ἑκάστῳ is ‘with each head’, the dative of κράς, ‘head’. φῶτ’ is φῶτα, ‘a man’, and ἐξαρπάξασα the aorist participle of ἐξαρπάζω ‘snatch out’. νεός is the Ionic genitive of ναῦς and κυανοπρῴροιο the genitive of κυανόπρῳρος ‘dark-prowed’. Circe’s speech goes on beyond this part, so the English does not close the single mark here.
